title: The Lesson I Learned From Elihu
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Elihu
The voice nobody expected. The truth nobody wanted. The moment that changed everything.
There are moments in life when suffering feels louder than God.
Moments when prayers bounce off the ceiling.
Moments when grief sits at the dinner table.
Moments when disappointment becomes your closest companion.
You open your Bible searching for answers, but your heart is asking a deeper question:
"God, where are You?"
That question is as old as humanity itself.
And hidden in one of the most overlooked portions of Scripture is a man whose voice still echoes through every season of confusion, pain, disappointment, and unanswered questions.
His name was Elihu.
Most Christians know Job.
Many know Job's three friends.
Few remember Elihu.
Yet the lesson I learned from him may be one of the most life-changing truths I have ever discovered.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle between us and God is not rebellion.
It is assuming we already understand Him.
The story unfolds in the Book of Job, a book that wrestles with suffering more honestly than perhaps any other book in Scripture.
Job had lost everything.
His children.
His wealth.
His health.
His reputation.
His future.
And after chapters of endless debate between Job and his friends, something remarkable happens.
A young man finally speaks.
His name, אֱלִיהוּ (Eliyhu), means "My God is He."
Unlike Job's friends, Elihu does not simply accuse.
Unlike Job, he does not justify himself.
Instead, he points everyone back to the greatness of God.
And that is where the lesson begins.
Many people approach suffering with only two options.
Either God is unfair.
Or God owes them an explanation.
Elihu challenges both assumptions.
In Job 33:14 he declares:
"For God speaks once, and twice, yet man does not perceive it."
The Hebrew word translated "speaks" is יְדַבֶּר (yedabber), implying ongoing communication.
Elihu's point is stunning.
God is not silent.
We are often unable to recognize His voice.
That realization hit me harder than I expected.
How many times have I accused God of silence while drowning out His voice with fear?
How many times have I demanded answers while ignoring His presence?
How many times have I mistaken God's hiddenness for His absence?
Elihu understood something many believers still struggle to understand.
God's greatest work is often happening when we cannot see it.
The lesson becomes even more profound when Elihu speaks about suffering itself.
Modern culture teaches us to avoid pain at all costs.
Scripture teaches something deeper.
Not that pain is good.
But that God can redeem what pain intends to destroy.
Elihu says:
"He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by adversity." (Job 36:15)
Think about that.
Not merely despite suffering.
Through suffering.
The Hebrew idea suggests that affliction can become a doorway through which God gains our attention.
Many of us can testify to this reality.
We met God in hospital rooms.
We encountered Him after divorce papers arrived.
We found Him after funerals.
We discovered His faithfulness when our own strength collapsed.
The very season we wanted removed became the season that revealed Him most clearly.
That is not because God delights in pain.
It is because redemption is His specialty.
The entire Gospel is built upon that truth.
The cross was history's greatest scandal.
Yet through that scandal came grace.
Through suffering came salvation.
Through death came life.
Through apparent defeat came eternal victory.
That is why our theme remains timeless:
Elihu's greatest contribution comes near the end of his speech.
He repeatedly points Job away from himself and toward God's majesty.
In Job 37:14 he says:
"Stand still and consider the wondrous works of God."
The phrase "stand still" comes from the Hebrew root עָמַד (amad), meaning to stop, remain, endure, or take one's position.
In other words:
Stop striving.
Stop demanding.
Stop controlling.
Stop assuming.
Pause long enough to behold God again.
What if the breakthrough you're seeking is not another explanation?
What if it is a greater vision of God Himself?
That is exactly where Elihu leads Job.
And it is exactly where the Gospel leads us.
The New Testament reveals this truth even more clearly.
When Jesus calmed storms, healed the sick, raised the dead, forgave sinners, and ultimately rose from the grave, He was revealing something humanity desperately needed to see.
God is not merely powerful.
He is good.
The Greek word often translated as grace is χάρις (charis).
It means favor, gift, kindness freely given.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Not purchased.
Given.
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Job could not yet see the cross.
Elihu could not yet see Calvary.
But both point toward the same reality.
A God whose wisdom exceeds human understanding.
A God whose purposes reach beyond temporary suffering.
A God whose mercy triumphs over our worst failures.
A God who enters our pain rather than abandoning us to it.
Jesus Christ is the ultimate answer to the questions Elihu raises.
Not because He explains every mystery.
But because He reveals the heart of God.
The lesson I learned from Elihu is simple, but it changed everything.
God does not owe me complete understanding.
He invites me into complete trust.
There is a difference.
Understanding demands sight.
Trust walks by faith.
Understanding seeks control.
Trust surrenders.
Understanding ends when answers disappear.
Trust remains when answers never come.
And if you're reading this while carrying disappointment, confusion, grief, unanswered prayers, financial struggles, broken relationships, hidden wounds, or silent battles, hear this clearly:
Your story is not finished.
The same God who spoke through Elihu still speaks.
The same God who sustained Job still sustains.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead is still rewriting stories today.
Maybe that's why Elihu's words continue to matter.
Because every generation eventually discovers what Job discovered.
Life will bring questions.
God will remain faithful.
And faith grows strongest when it learns to trust His character more than its circumstances.
Perhaps the greatest miracle is not receiving every answer we seek.
Perhaps the greatest miracle is discovering that Jesus remains enough even when answers never arrive.
Someone scrolling through despair today may be one share away from hearing exactly what they need.
You never know how God may use a simple act of obedience to change a life.
What season taught you to trust God more deeply?
What lesson did suffering teach you about Jesus?
Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
It is one of the most practical ways to help expand this ministry's reach while glorifying God through the spread of biblical truth.
Because one day you may need to remember what Elihu taught Job.
Sometimes God's greatest answer is not an explanation.
Sometimes His greatest answer is Himself.
And when Jesus is the answer, even the darkest chapter can become the beginning of redemption.
The God who seemed silent was writing a better ending all along.
